overview: This four-page Department of State “List of Papers,” compiled for decimal file 894.918 on restriction of the press in Japan, indexes correspondence and reports dating from 1930 to 1937. The entries document an expanding system of press bans, military and naval censorship, controls on foreign correspondents and news services, suppression of publications deemed inflammatory or diplomatically harmful, confiscation of imported books and magazines, and restrictions connected with Japanese operations in Manchuria, Manchukuo, China, and other strategic areas. Especially prominent are reports from Ambassadors W. Cameron Forbes and Joseph C. Grew, the suppression of the May 1936 issue of Current History, and measures anticipating wartime mobilization and secrecy.

subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers for File 894.918
subfiles.about: A four-page index of reports, telegrams, memoranda, and correspondence concerning Japanese press restrictions and censorship from 1930 through 1937.
subfiles.summary: The list traces increasingly broad Japanese controls over reporting, beginning with political and military press bans and extending to troop movements, naval and aviation information, foreign affairs, news services, cartoons, correspondents, imported books, and foreign magazines. It records the suppression of material concerning Manchuria, Manchukuo, China, the February 26 Incident, and sensitive defense measures in Taiwan, the Bonin Islands, North Korea, and Japan’s southwestern islands. Several entries provide cross-references to documents filed elsewhere, while a substantial sequence follows the confiscation of the May 1936 issue of Current History because of Charles Hodges’s article “Japanese Enigma.” The final entries concern excluded American magazines and the suppression of the Japan Advertiser for advocating Japanese neutrality in a future world war.

interest: The index is valuable as a compact chronology of the Japanese government’s movement toward comprehensive information control during the 1930s. It links censorship of domestic political and military news with restrictions on foreign journalists, imported publications, diplomatic commentary, and representations of foreign rulers. Its summaries and decimal-file cross-references also provide a research map to records filed under military affairs, foreign relations, propaganda, and Manchurian subjects rather than solely under press censorship.
